records.title: The Children of Lir (Oidheadh Chloinne Lir)
records.summary: A cornerstone of Ireland's Mythological Cycle, King Lir of the Tuatha Dé Danann has four beautiful children—Fionnuala, Aodh, Fiachra, and Conn—with his beloved wife. Following her death, their jealous stepmother Aoife uses a druidic rod to transform the children into four singing white swans, condemning them to spend nine hundred years on Ireland's waters: three hundred on Lough Derravaragh, three hundred on the stormy Sea of Moyle, and three hundred on the icy Atlantic waters of Inis Glóire. Only the arrival of Christianity and the sound of the first chapel bell can break the spell, restoring them as ancient, withered mortals who receive baptism before passing peacefully into the heavens.
alternate_names: The Fate of the Children of Lir
records.historical_period: Mythological Cycle (oral tradition compiled in Early Modern Irish c. 15th Century)

records.title: The Salmon of Knowledge (Bradán Feasa)
records.summary: The wise druid and poet Finnegas spent seven patient years fishing the River Boyne for the legendary Salmon of Knowledge (Bradán Feasa), which fed on the magical hazel nuts of the Well of Segais, bestowing all worldly wisdom upon whoever ate its flesh. When Finnegas finally captures the creature, he commands his young apprentice, Fionn Mac Cumhaill, to cook it on a spit, forbidding him from tasting a single morsel. While turning the fish, Fionn burns his thumb on a hot blister on the skin and instinctively sucks on the thumb to relieve the pain. Instantly absorbing the cosmic wisdom of the universe, Fionn becomes the legendary leader of the Fianna warriors.
alternate_names: Fionn and the Salmon of Wisdom
records.historical_period: Fenian Cycle (c. 12th Century compilation Acallam na Senórach)

records.title: Oisin in the Land of Youth (Tír na nÓg)
records.summary: The great warrior-poet Oisín, son of Fionn Mac Cumhaill, is swept across the western sea atop a white fairy steed by the golden-haired princess Niamh Chinn Óir to Tír na nÓg, the enchanted realm of eternal youth where sorrow, age, and death are unknown. After what feels like three blissfully happy years, Oisín longs to visit his comrades in Ireland. Niamh grants him the magical horse, warning that if his feet ever touch mortal soil, he can never return. Arriving in Ireland, Oisín discovers three hundred years have passed and the Fianna are mere legends. While leaning from his saddle to assist peasants lifting a boulder, his stirrup snaps; touching the earth, he instantly withers into a blind, dying old man.
records.historical_period: Fenian Cycle (popularized in 18th-century poem by Mícheál Coimín)
records.region_or_community: County Kerry and Western Atlantic Seaboard

records.title: Cu Chulainn and the Hound of Culann
records.summary: Arriving late at a festive feast hosted by the blacksmith Culann for King Conchobar of Ulster, the seven-year-old boy warrior Sétanta is ambushed by Culann's monstrous watch-hound, capable of tearing an army to pieces. Unarmed, Sétanta drives a bronze hurling ball (sliotar) down the beast's throat with his hurley and shatters its skull against a stone pillar. Seeing the blacksmith weeping over the loss of his guardian, the boy pledges to guard Culann's fortress himself until a new hound can be raised, earning the hero-name Cú Chulainn—'The Hound of Culann'—and beginning the epic saga of Ulster's greatest champion.
records.historical_period: Ulster Cycle (c. 1st Century CE setting, recorded 11th Century Book of the Dun Cow)
records.region_or_community: Cooley Peninsula, County Louth and Armagh

records.title: Finn MacCool and the Giant's Causeway
records.summary: When the Scottish giant Benandonner challenges the Irish champion Finn MacCool across the North Channel, Finn builds a colossal causeway of hexagonal basalt pillars across the sea from County Antrim to Staffa so the two can duel. Sighting Benandonner approaching, Finn realizes his rival is vastly larger than expected. Finn's clever wife Oonagh disguises him in baby clothes inside an enormous cradle. When Benandonner arrives, Oonagh serves him iron griddle-cakes baked inside bread and shows him the giant 'baby.' Terrified at how colossal the father of such a gigantic infant must be, Benandonner flees back to Scotland, tearing up the causeway behind him.
alternate_names: The Legend of the Giant's Causeway
records.historical_period: Early Modern Irish Folklore (widespread oral tradition recorded 18th Century)

records.title: The Keen of the Banshee (Bean Sídhe)
records.summary: Deeply rooted in ancient Gaelic ancestral traditions, the Bean Sídhe (Woman of the Fairy Mounds) is an ethereal spirit bound to the five noble Gaelic lineages: the O'Neills, O'Briens, O'Connors, O'Gradys, and Kavanaghs. Appearing as a sorrowful maiden, a noble matron, or a withered crone clad in green or grey robes with wild silver hair, she is rarely seen but heard at dead of night. Her piercing, desolate keen (caoineadh) echoes over fields, bogs, and rivers to lament and forewarn the imminent death of a family member, reminding mortals of the thin veil separating the living from the Otherworld.
alternate_names: The Death Messenger of the Gael
records.region_or_community: Munster, Connacht, and Leinster Gaelic lineages
community_attributions: Irish scéalaí and rural folklore collectors

records.title: The Leprechaun of Carlingford and the Pot of Gold
records.summary: Solitary fairy craftsmen known as leipreacháin dwell along the slopes of the Cooley Mountains in County Louth, renowned as cobblers to the Good People and guardians of buried crocks of Danish gold. When a quick-witted farm lad catches one tapping an awl beneath a dock leaf, he grasps the sprite tightly, knowing that if he breaks eye contact for an instant, the fairy will vanish. The leprechaun leads him to a ragwort bush in a vast field, promising the treasure lies buried below. The lad ties a bright red garter to the weed and dashes home for a spade, only to return and find every single ragwort plant in the sixty-acre field tied with an identical red garter.
records.region_or_community: Carlingford and Cooley Peninsula, County Louth
community_attributions: Irish Fairy and Folk Tale collectors

records.title: The Selkie Bride of Galway Bay
records.summary: Walking along the rocky shores of Galway Bay on a midsummer evening, a lonely fisherman watches a group of seals shed their sleek pelts upon the sea-wrack and dance in human form as radiant women. Captivated, he conceals one of the seal skins beneath the thatch of his cottage roof, compelling the maiden to remain and become his wife. Although she bears him children and cares for his home with gentle tenderness, her gaze remains forever fixed on the crashing surf. Years later, her youngest child discovers the hidden pelt in the rafters; slipping the skin over her shoulders, she transforms back into a seal, plunging into the Atlantic with a sorrowful farewell.
records.region_or_community: Connemara and Aran Islands, County Galway

records.title: The Fairy Forts and Fairy Raths of Munster
records.summary: Scattered by the tens of thousands across the Irish countryside, ancient circular earthworks and ringforts (raths and lisses) from the Iron Age are venerated in rural folklore as the subterranean fortresses of the Aos Sí (the Fairy Folk). Irish countryfolk adhere to an unwritten law: never fell a lone hawthorn fairy thorn tree, nor bulldoze the banks of a rath, lest devastating misfortune, cattle disease, or death fall upon the household. Even during modern construction, road routes across Ireland have been famously diverted around fairy forts to respect the ancient dwellings of the Otherworld.
alternate_names: The Homes of the Good People
records.historical_period: Ancient Iron Age Monuments, Sustained Medieval to Contemporary Lore
records.region_or_community: Munster and Connacht rural farming communities

records.title: The Voyage of Saint Brendan the Navigator
records.summary: Setting sail from the foot of Mount Brandon in County Kerry in a leather currach with fourteen monk companions, Saint Brendan embarked on a seven-year voyage across the uncharted Atlantic Ocean in search of the Promised Land of the Saints. En route, the travelers encounter magical floating islands of crystal (icebergs), pillars of fire hurled by demons (volcanoes), and make camp upon a peaceful island to celebrate Easter Mass, only to discover the island is Jasconius, an immense sea monster that submerges beneath them. Blending early Christian monastic peregrinatio with ancient Gaelic immram voyage mythology, the epic chronicles Ireland's greatest maritime legend.
records.historical_period: Early Christian Ireland (c. 6th Century setting, written c. 9th Century)
